data.name: Casa Luca de Tena
data.description: The Casa Luca de Tena is a building in the Spanish city of Seville , the result of a project by the architect Aníbal González and whose construction was completed in 1926. It is listed in the General Catalogue of Andalusian Historical Heritage.

data.name: Parroquia Corpus Christi
data.style: Regionalist with classical and Baroque influences
data.description: Religious building dedicated to Christian worship. It was founded by separating part of the congregations belonging to the parishes of El Sagrario and San Bernardo. The first stone of the church was laid in 1931, and construction began immediately; Cardinal Ilundain Esteban solemnly consecrated it on April 1, 1933. The original design was never fully completed, which is especially noticeable in the façade, which remains unfinished.

data.name: RACA 14 - Regimiento de Artillería de Campaña nº 14 (Acuartelamiento Daoiz y Velarde)
data.style: Regionalist / eclectic military style of early 20th century
data.description: An important military artillery barracks in Seville, with more than 60 years of active use, and today it is an emblematic site undergoing urban transformation after decades of abandonment.

data.name: Acuartelamiento Vigil de Quiñones - Hospital Militar Queipo de Llano - Hospital de La Legión
data.style: Functionalist Military Architecture with Rationalist influences
data.description: The Vigil de Quiñones Barracks was built in 1937 as the Queipo de Llano Military Hospital, remaining in operation until the opening of the Vigil de Quiñones Military Hospital in 1980. After that, it continued to provide medical and psychiatric services until 1983, when it was converted into a military barracks to house command units and troops.

data.name: Antiguo Cuartel Alfonso XIII
data.style: Functional military building with eclectic and Mudejar elements
data.description: Built around 1928 as a cavalry barracks, it served as an important military base for the Regimiento de Caballería Sagunto 7 and other units, reflecting early 20th-century Spanish military architecture.

data.name: la Casa Rosa (Villa Eugenia)
data.style: French-influenced eclectic with regional Spanish elements
data.district: Distrito Sur La Palmera / Parque de María Luisa
data.address: Av. de la Guardia Civil, 1, 41013 Sevilla
data.description: Built in 1894 for the Marquesa de Angulo, Villa Eugenia (Casa Rosa) is a historic palacete with French and regional influences, expanded in 1916 and 1927, and linked to the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition.

data.name: Pabellón de México (Exposición Iberoamericana de Sevilla 1929)
data.district: Distrito Sur La Palmera / Parque de María Luisa
data.address: P.º de las Delicias, s/n, 41013 Sevilla
data.description: El Pabellon de Mexico was built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition in Seville to showcase Mexico’s culture, featuring Neoindigenist architecture inspired by Mayan and Toltec motifs. Today, it is preserved as a historic building and is used by the University of Seville for academic and cultural purposes.

data.name: Pabellón de Colombia (Exposición Iberoamericana de Sevilla 1929)
data.style: Eclectic / Neoindigenist with pre‑Columbian decorative elements
data.district: Distrito Sur La Palmera / Parque de María Luisa
data.address: P.º de las Delicias, s/n, 41012 Sevilla
data.description: El Pabellon de Colombia was built for the 1929 Ibero‑American Exposition in Seville to represent Colombian culture and industry. Designed by Spanish architect José Granados de la Vega, it features eclectic architecture enriched with decorative elements inspired by pre‑Columbian art. Today it is preserved as a historic building and serves as the Consulate General of Colombia in Seville.

data.name: Pabellón de Marruecos (Exposición Iberoamericana de Sevilla 1929)
data.district: Distrito Sur / Parque de María Luisa
data.description: The Moroccan Pavilion was built for the 1929 Ibero‑American Exposition in Seville to represent aspects of Moroccan culture and architecture. Designed by José Gutiérrez Lescura with artistic input from Mariano Bertuchi, its design incorporates traditional Moroccan and Moorish elements such as horseshoe arches and decorative tilework. After the exposition, the building was repurposed as the Administrative Service of Parks and Gardens of the Seville City Council, and it remains a preserved historic building reflecting cross‑cultural architectural heritage.

data.name: Pabellón de Brasil (Exposición Iberoamericana de Sevilla 1929)
data.district: Distrito Sur / Parque de María Luisa
data.address: P.º de las Delicias, s/n, 41012 Sevilla
data.description: Pabellón de Brasil was built for the 1929 Ibero‑American Exposition in Seville to showcase Brazilian culture and industry. Designed by architect Pedro Paulo Bernardes Vastos in a neo‑Baroque style inspired by Brazil’s colonial cities, it was later adapted for other uses and is currently owned by the University of Seville as a preserved historic building.

data.name: Pabellón Real (Sevilla)
data.style: Neo-Gothic historicist with Sevillian Regionalism elements
data.district: Distrito Sur / Parque de María Luisa
data.address: P.º de las Delicias, s/n, 41012 Sevilla
data.description: The Pabellón Real was built between 1912 and 1916 for exhibition purposes and later integrated into the Ibero-American Exposition of 1929. Designed by Aníbal González, it features Neo-Gothic historicist architecture with Sevillian Regionalism elements. Today it is preserved and used for municipal offices and cultural purposes, maintaining its historic and architectural significance.

data.name: Pabellón Domecq (Exposición Iberoamericana de Sevilla 1929)
data.district: Distrito Sur / Parque de María Luisa
data.description: The Domecq Pavilion was built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition in Seville as the exhibition space for the Jerez winery Domecq. Designed by architect Aurelio Gómez Millán, the building is neoclassical in brick and combines regionalist elements. After the exposition it served various institutional uses and, since 1998, has been the home of Juventudes Musicales, hosting cultural events and concerts.

data.name: Pabellón de Arte Antiguo (Exposición Iberoamericana de Sevilla 1929)
data.style: Mudéjar Revival / Brick and ceramic decorative architecture
data.district: Distrito Sur / Parque de María Luisa
data.address: Plaza de América, Parque de María Luisa, 41013 Sevilla
data.description: The Pavilion of Ancient Art was originally planned as the Pavilion of Industries, Manufactures and Decorative Arts for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition in Seville. Designed and built in 1914 by architect Aníbal González, it features brick construction with ceramic decoration and is known locally as the Mudéjar Pavilion. Today it houses the Museo de Artes y Costumbres Populares, preserving its historical and architectural legacy.

data.name: Museo Arqueológico Provincial de Sevilla
data.district: Distrito Sur / Parque de María Luisa
data.description: The Provincial Archaeological Museum of Seville was founded in 1879 and since 1946 has been housed in the former Pavilion of Fine Arts of the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition. Designed by Aníbal González in a Neo-Renaissance (Plateresque) style, the museum preserves extensive archaeological collections from the province.

data.name: Pabellón de Argentina (Exposición Iberoamericana de Sevilla 1929)
data.address: P.º de las Delicias, s/n, 41012 Sevilla
data.description: The Argentine Pavilion is a historic exhibition building constructed for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition in Seville. Designed by architect Martín Noel, it represents Argentina through a Hispano-American Neo-Baroque style and today it is used as a dance conservatory.

data.name: Pabellón de Guatemala (Exposición Iberoamericana de Sevilla 1929)
data.address: P.º de las Delicias, s/n, 41012 Sevilla
data.description: The Guatemalan Pavilion at the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition in Seville features an eclectic architectural style with strong influences from Central American indigenous art. Its exterior is decorated with blue and white tiles inspired by Mayan motifs and the Guatemalan flag, combining historicist regionalism with traditional design elements.

data.name: Plaza de España
data.style: Spanish Regionalist Historicist style with Renaissance, Baroque, and Mudéjar influences
data.address: Parque de María Luisa, s/n, 41013 Sevilla, Spain
data.description: The Plaza de España in Seville is a monumental public complex built within the Parque de María Luisa for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition. Designed by Aníbal González, it features a semi-circular palace with galleries, towers, bridges over a central canal, and decorative benches representing each Spanish province. It combines Renaissance, Baroque, and Mudéjar influences, serving as both a symbolic and administrative structure for exhibitions and government offices.

data.name: Costurero de la Reina
data.address: P.º de las Delicias, Casco Antiguo, 41012 Sevilla
data.description: The Costurero de la Reina is a small, historic building located in the Parque de María Luisa in Seville. Built in 1893 by architect José Hernández in a Neo-Mudéjar style, it was originally a sewing room for Queen Maria Cristina. The building is notable for its delicate brickwork, decorative towers, and ornamental windows, representing a picturesque example of late 19th-century Sevillian architecture.

data.name: Pabellón de Estados Unidos (Exposición Iberoamericana de Sevilla 1929)
data.address: P.º de las Delicias, 7, Casco Antiguo, 41013 Sevilla
data.description: The United States Pavilion, designed by architect William Templeton Johnson for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition in Seville, is a notable example of American Colonial Revival, with influences from Neoclassicism and Spanish colonial architecture. Its design features symmetrical façades, classical columns, and elegant pediments, conveying sobriety and harmony. The pavilion aimed to project American historical tradition through an architectural language that blends colonial heritage with a modern interpretation, harmonizing with the Hispanic context of the exposition.

data.name: Pabellón de Uruguay (Exposición Iberoamericana de Sevilla 1929)
data.address: Av. de Chile, s/n, Casco Antiguo, 41013 Sevilla
data.description: The Uruguay Pavilion, designed for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition in Seville, is a prominent example of Uruguayan Neo-Colonial style, inspired by Spanish colonial architecture. Its façade features round arches, ornate columns, and tile decoration, evoking Hispanic tradition with a modern approach. The pavilion reflects the intent to project Uruguayan national identity through an architectural language that blends historical heritage and modernity, in harmony with the spirit of the exposition.

data.name: Pabellón de Chile (Exposición Iberoamericana de Sevilla 1929)
data.district: Distrito Sur / Parque de María Luisa
data.address: Pabellón de Chile, Av. de Chile, 1, Casco Antiguo, 41013 Sevilla
data.description: The Chilean Pavilion was built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition in Seville to represent Chilean culture and progress. Designed by architect Juan Martínez Gutiérrez, it combines neo-colonial influences with modern construction techniques. Today it is preserved and used for institutional purposes.

data.name: Pabellón de Perú (Exposición Iberoamericana de Sevilla 1929)
data.district: Distrito Sur / Parque de María Luisa
data.address: Av. de María Luisa, s/n, Casco Antiguo, 41013 Sevilla
data.description: The Peruvian Pavilion was built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition in Seville and designed by architect and sculptor Manuel Piqueras Cotolí. Its architecture reflects a neo-indigenist style inspired by pre-Columbian and colonial Peruvian art. Today the building is preserved and serves cultural and institutional functions.

data.name: Casino de la Exposición
data.district: Distrito Sur / Parque de María Luisa
data.address: Gta. San Diego, S/N, Casco Antiguo, 41013 Sevilla
data.description: The Casino de la Exposición was built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition in Seville as a social and leisure space. Designed by architect Aníbal González, it features regionalist architecture with Renaissance influences. Today it functions as a cultural and event venue.

data.name: Pabellón de Cristal (Exposición Iberoamericana de Sevilla 1929)
data.district: Distrito Sur / Parque de María Luisa
data.address: P.º de las Delicias, s/n, 41013 Sevilla
data.description: The Crystal Pavilion was built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition in Seville. Designed by José Espiau y Muñoz, it features a striking glass and iron structure that exemplifies modernist exhibition architecture of the period. It was intended as a light, transparent space for displays and events, and is preserved as part of the historical heritage of the exposition.

data.architect: Carlos y Guilherme Rebelo de Andrade
data.name: Pabellón de Portugal (Exposición Iberoamericana de Sevilla 1929)
data.district: Distrito Sur / Parque de María Luisa
data.description: The Portuguese Pavilion was built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition in Seville to represent Portugal’s national identity. Its architecture draws inspiration from historicist and Neo-Manueline styles. The building has been preserved and adapted for institutional use.

data.name: Real Fábrica de Tabacos de Sevilla
data.description: The Royal Tobacco Factory of Seville was built in the 18th century and is one of the largest industrial buildings of its time in Europe. Designed by Sebastián Van der Borcht, it reflects Baroque industrial architecture. Today it houses the University of Seville.

data.name: Palacio de San Telmo
data.description: The Palace of San Telmo is a monumental Baroque building originally constructed as a nautical college. Designed by Leonardo de Figueroa, it later became a royal residence and today serves as the headquarters of the Presidency of the Andalusian Government.

data.name: Torre del Oro
data.address: Paseo de Cristóbal Colón, s/n, 41001 Sevilla
data.description: The Torre del Oro is a historic watchtower built during the Almohad period to control access to Seville via the Guadalquivir River. It is one of the city’s most iconic monuments and currently houses a maritime museum.

data.name: Hotel Alfonso XIII
data.description: The Hotel Alfonso XIII was built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition in Seville to accommodate distinguished guests. Designed by José Espiau y Muñoz, it is one of the most luxurious historic hotels in Spain and a landmark of Sevillian regionalist architecture.

data.name: Real Alcázar de Sevilla
data.description: The Royal Alcázar of Seville is a historic royal palace originally developed from an Islamic fortress. It is one of the oldest palaces still in use in Europe and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, showcasing a unique blend of Islamic, Mudéjar, Gothic, Renaissance, and Baroque styles.

data.name: Capilla de Santa María de Jesús
data.address: Av. de la Constitución, 27, Casco Antiguo, 41004 Sevilla
data.description: The Chapel of Santa María de Jesús was built in the 17th century and is a notable example of Sevillian Baroque architecture. It is linked to the Hermandad de la Vera Cruz and features richly decorated altarpieces and religious artworks.

data.architect: Juan de Herrera el Mozo (interior contributions by Valdés Leal & Murillo)
data.name: Hospital de la Caridad
data.description: The Hospital de la Caridad is a 17th-century charitable institution, famous for its Baroque interior, paintings by Murillo, and works by Valdés Leal. It continues to represent the tradition of Sevillian philanthropy and Baroque art.

data.name: Archivo General de Indias
data.address: Av. de la Constitución, s/n, 41004 Sevilla
data.description: The General Archive of the Indies houses valuable documents related to the Spanish colonies in the Americas. Designed by Juan de Herrera, the building is a Renaissance architectural masterpiece and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

data.name: Plaza de Toros de la Real Maestranza de Caballería de Sevilla
data.address: Paseo de Cristóbal Colón, s/n, 41001 Sevilla
data.description: The Royal Bullring of Seville, one of the most famous in Spain, was founded in the 18th century. It features Baroque architecture and is still active for bullfighting events, serving as a cultural symbol of the city.

data.name: Catedral de Sevilla
data.address: Avenida de la Constitución, s/n, 41004 Sevilla
data.description: Seville Cathedral, the largest Gothic cathedral in the world, was built over the former Almohad mosque. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and houses remarkable artworks, chapels, and the tomb of Christopher Columbus.

data.name: La Giralda
data.address: Avenida de la Constitución, s/n, 41004 Sevilla
data.description: La Giralda is the bell tower of Seville Cathedral, originally built as an Almohad minaret in the 12th century. It was later topped with Renaissance elements and is one of the most iconic landmarks of the city.

data.name: Palacio Arzobispal de Sevilla
data.description: The Archbishop's Palace of Seville was originally constructed in the late 16th century and has undergone modifications in Renaissance and Baroque styles. It serves as the residence of the Archbishop of Seville and is an important historic and architectural landmark in the city, located next to the Cathedral and La Giralda.

data.name: Palacio de las Dueñas
data.description: The Palace of Las Dueñas is a historic palace blending Gothic, Mudéjar, and Renaissance styles. It has been a residence of noble families and contains an important collection of art and furniture.

data.name: Casa Fabiola
data.district: Distrito Sur / Parque de María Luisa
data.description: Casa Fabiola is a private historic residence designed in eclectic and regionalist style. Built in the early 20th century, it is an example of Sevillian residential architecture influenced by the Ibero-American Exposition era.

data.name: Casa Palacio del Pumarejo
data.description: The Casa Palacio del Pumarejo is a historic palace from the 18th century in Seville. It is an important example of Baroque residential architecture and has been preserved as a cultural heritage site.

data.architect: Enrique Egas / Fadrique Enríquez de Rivera
data.name: Casa de Pilatos
data.description: Casa de Pilatos is a historic palace in Seville blending Andalusian Renaissance and Mudéjar architecture. Built in the late 15th century and modified over the 16th century, it is known for its patios, marble columns, azulejos, and exquisite art collection, representing a perfect mix of Italian Renaissance and Spanish traditions.

data.name: Iglesia de San Marcos
data.description: The Church of San Marcos is one of the oldest parish churches in Seville, built around 1356 after the Christian reconquest, likely over the remains of an earlier mosque. It is a notable example of Gothic-Mudéjar architecture, combining brick construction, pointed arches, and Mudéjar decorative elements. The church has undergone several restorations over the centuries and remains an important religious and historical landmark in the city.

data.name: Real Parroquia de Señora Santa Ana
data.description: The Royal Parish Church of Our Lady Saint Anne, known as Santa Ana de Triana, is the oldest Christian church built in Seville after the Castilian conquest. Construction began in 1266 by order of King Alfonso X the Wise, combining early Gothic structure with Mudéjar decorative elements. It is considered the cathedral of Triana and holds significant religious, artistic, and historical importance, housing valuable Gothic sculptures and altarpieces.

data.name: Iglesia de San Gil
data.description: The Church of San Gil is a 14th-century parish church built after the 1356 earthquake as part of Seville’s Gothic-Mudéjar parish network. Constructed primarily in brick, it features pointed arches, Mudéjar decorative elements, and later Baroque additions. The church is closely linked to the religious life of the Macarena area and is historically associated with several Sevillian brotherhoods.

data.name: Iglesia de San Román
data.address: Pl. San Román, 3, Casco Antiguo, 41003 Sevilla
data.description: The Church of San Román is a 14th-century parish church rebuilt after the 1356 earthquake, occupying the site of a former mosque. It is a representative example of Sevillian Gothic-Mudéjar architecture, characterized by brick construction, pointed arches, and Mudéjar decorative elements. The church later incorporated Baroque features and today houses the Parish of San Román and Santa Catalina.

data.name: Iglesia de Santa Marina
data.description: The Church of Santa Marina is one of the oldest Christian churches in Seville, built around 1265 after the reconquest. It combines Gothic and Mudéjar elements, with brick construction, pointed arches, and historical chapels. The church has undergone restorations but retains its medieval character and remains an important religious and historical site in the Casco Antiguo.

data.name: Iglesia de Omnium Sanctorum
data.description: The Church of Omnium Sanctorum in Seville is one of the oldest Christian parish churches in the city, built around 1249 shortly after the Christian reconquest. It combines Mudéjar and Gothic elements, reusing parts of the former mosque’s structure and preserving its medieval character despite later renovations.

data.name: Iglesia de San Esteban
data.address: Calle San Esteban, 1, Casco Antiguo, 41003 Sevilla
data.description: The Church of San Esteban in Seville is a Gothic‑Mudéjar parish church dating from the 14th century, built on the site of a former mosque. It features three naves, Gothic stone portals, and a later tower with an 18th‑century bell, following reconstruction after the Lisbon earthquake. Inside, important retablos and artworks are preserved, including pieces by Zurbarán and the Polanco brothers.

data.name: Basílica de la Macarena
data.address: Pl. de la Esperanza Macarena, 1, Casco Antiguo, 41002 Sevilla
data.description: The Basilica of Santa María de la Esperanza Macarena in Seville is a Catholic temple built between 1941 and 1949 to house the images of the Hermandad de la Esperanza Macarena. Designed by architect Aurelio Gómez Millán in a Baroque/neo‑Baroque style, it features a single nave with side chapels and was later consecrated in 1966. It was granted the dignity of Minor Basilica by Pope Paul VI, becoming the first Sevillian church with that title and remains one of the city’s most iconic religious sites.

data.name: Iglesia de San Luis de los Franceses
data.description: The Church of San Luis de los Franceses in Seville is a masterpiece of Sevillian Baroque architecture built for the Jesuit novitiate. Construction began in 1699 and was completed in 1731 under the direction of architect Leonardo de Figueroa. The interior features outstanding retablos by Pedro Duque Cornejo and frescoes by Lucas Valdés, representing one of the city’s most remarkable Baroque churches.

data.name: Real Parroquia de Santa María Magdalena, de Sevilla
data.description: The Church of Santa María Magdalena in Seville is a prominent Baroque parish church whose current structure was built between 1691 and 1709 on the site of the former medieval parish, under the design of architect Leonardo de Figueroa. It features a richly decorated interior with notable murals, retablos, and artistic works, and remains an important historical and cultural landmark in the city.

data.name: Iglesia de Santa María la Blanca
data.address: Calle Santa María la Blanca, 5, 41004 Sevilla
data.description: The Church of Santa María la Blanca in Seville occupies the site of a former synagogue and was transformed into a Christian church after 1391. The current Baroque configuration dates mainly from the reconstruction between 1660 and 1665 under Juan González, with notable interior decoration including plasterwork and paintings. It remains a significant historic parish church in the old Jewish quarter.

data.name: Iglesia de San Lorenzo
data.address: Pl. S. Lorenzo, 7, Casco Antiguo, 41002 Sevilla
data.description: The Church of San Lorenzo in Seville is a historic parish church originally constructed in the 14th century in a Gothic‑Mudéjar style. Over the centuries it was significantly modified, with Baroque additions in the 17th and 18th centuries. The building houses a remarkable artistic heritage including a major altarpiece begun by Martínez Montañés and completed by the Rivas brothers.

data.architect: Alberto Balbontín Orta & Antonio Delgado Roig
data.name: Basílica de Jesús del Gran Poder
data.description: The Basilica of Jesús del Gran Poder in Seville is a 20th‑century temple built between 1960 and 1965 to house the devotion to Nuestro Padre Jesús del Gran Poder. Designed by architects Alberto Balbontín Orta and Antonio Delgado Roig in a historicist/neo‑Baroque style, it was consecrated in 1965 and later granted the title of Minor Basilica by Pope John Paul II in 1992. The basilica preserves the famous Baroque image of Jesús del Gran Poder carved by Juan de Mesa in 1620 and is one of the city’s most important religious landmarks.

data.name: Iglesia Colegial del Divino Salvador
data.address: Pl. del Salvador, 3, Casco Antiguo, 41004 Sevilla
data.description: The Iglesia del Divino Salvador is a major Baroque church in Seville, originally built on the site of a former mosque. Designed by Leonardo de Figueroa in the late 17th century, it features a richly decorated interior with altarpieces, sculptures, and paintings, making it one of the most important religious landmarks in the city.

data.name: Iglesia de San Ildefonso
data.address: C. Rodríguez Marín, 2, Casco Antiguo, 41003 Sevilla
data.description: The Church of San Ildefonso in Seville is a neoclassical parish church whose construction began in 1794 and was completed in 1841, following designs by Julián Barnecilla and executed by architect José Echamorro. Notable for its monumental façade flanked by twin towers, the interior features three naves with a nave and transept and preserves artistic works including the retablo with images of San Ildefonso, San Pedro, and San Pablo.

data.name: Convento de Santa Paula
data.description: The Convent of Santa Paula in Seville is a historic monastery of the Hieronymite Order founded in 1475 and one of the city’s oldest monastic establishments. The convent church was built between 1483 and 1489 in a Gothic‑Mudéjar style, and the complex later received Baroque decorative additions. It contains cloisters, chapels, and a museum with works of art and religious heritage, and remains an active community of nuns in the heart of the old city.

data.name: Convento de San Leandro
data.style: Gothic‑Mudéjar origins with later Baroque elements
data.description: The Convent of San Leandro in Seville is an historic Augustinian convent founded in 1295. It occupies an important place in the city’s religious heritage and features a church constructed toward the end of the 16th century with later Baroque interior additions. The complex includes cloisters, chapels, and traditional monastic spaces, and is also known for its production of traditional sweets like yemas de San Leandro.

data.name: Convento de San Clemente
data.style: Medieval with later Renaissance and Baroque elements
data.description: The Convent of San Clemente in Seville is a historic Cistercian monastery founded in 1248 by King Fernando III the Saint after the conquest of the city. The complex, one of the oldest in Seville, developed architecturally across centuries with significant Renaissance‑period building phases and a church consecrated in 1588. The convent has a rich heritage including cloisters, Mudéjar and Baroque decorations, and is known for its historic art and monastic life.

data.name: Iglesia de San Jacinto
data.description: The Church of San Jacinto in the Triana district of Seville is an 18th‑century Baroque parish church. Built on the site of the former hermitage of La Candelaria after an earlier church collapsed in 1730, the current building was begun under Matías de Figueroa in the 1740s and inaugurated on January 29, 1775. It features a rectangular plan with three naves, a transept, and a dome with a drum, and is one of the notable Baroque churches in Triana.

data.architect: Diego de Riaño (original design), Juan Sánchez, Hernán Ruiz II
data.name: Ayuntamiento de Sevilla
data.style: Plateresque Renaissance with later Neoclassical additions
data.description: The City Hall of Seville is one of the most important Renaissance civic buildings in Spain. Construction began in 1527 under architect Diego de Riaño in an elaborate Plateresque Renaissance style, conceived to reflect Seville’s power and wealth as a major port of the Spanish Empire. The richly sculpted façades facing Plaza de San Francisco are among the finest examples of Plateresque decoration in Andalusia. In the 19th century, a Neoclassical façade was added facing Plaza Nueva, adapting the building to the new urban layout. Today, it continues to serve as the seat of the Seville City Council.

data.name: Edificio de La Adriática
data.style: Sevillian Regionalism with Neo-Mudéjar and Renaissance influences
data.description: The Adriática Building is one of the most emblematic examples of early 20th-century Sevillian Regionalist architecture. Designed by José Espiau y Muñoz for the insurance company La Adriática, its construction took place between 1914 and 1922. The building features rich decorative use of brick, ceramic tiles, wrought iron, and sculptural elements, blending Neo-Mudéjar and Renaissance influences. Its prominent corner tower and vertical emphasis made it a modern urban landmark in Seville at the time, symbolizing the city’s architectural renewal prior to the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition.

data.name: Banco de España (Sevilla)
data.description: The Bank of Spain building in Seville was constructed between 1925 and 1928 as the local headquarters of the Banco de España. Designed by architect Antonio Palacios Ramilo, one of the most prominent figures of Spanish monumental architecture of the early 20th century, the building reflects a sober and monumental eclectic style with strong Neoclassical influences. Its robust stone façade, symmetry, and classical composition convey stability, authority, and institutional power, aligning with the symbolic role of the Bank of Spain within the urban and economic landscape of Seville.

data.name: Capilla de San José
data.description: The Chapel of Saint Joseph in Seville is one of the finest examples of late Sevillian Baroque architecture. Construction began in 1699 under the direction of Pedro Romero and was completed in 1766 by Esteban Paredes. Although modest in size, the chapel is renowned for its extraordinarily rich interior decoration, featuring elaborate altarpieces, sculptural programs, polychrome plasterwork, and paintings by artists such as Lucas Valdés. Built by the Guild of Carpenters, the chapel reflects the devotional and artistic splendor of Baroque Seville and remains a highly significant religious and artistic landmark in the historic center.

data.name: Edificio de Telefónica (Sevilla)
data.style: Sevillian Regionalism with Renaissance and Baroque influences
data.description: The Telefónica Building in Seville was constructed between 1926 and 1929 as the headquarters of the Compañía Telefónica Nacional de España. Designed by architect Juan Talavera y Heredia, it is a notable example of Sevillian Regionalist architecture applied to a modern institutional and technological function. The building combines traditional materials such as brick, ceramics, and wrought iron with Renaissance and Baroque-inspired compositions, integrating modern infrastructure into the historic urban fabric of Plaza Nueva. It stands as a symbol of Seville’s modernization during the period leading up to the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition.

data.name: Casa Martín Nogueira
data.description: Casa Martín Nogueira in Seville is a historic residential building from the 1920s, designed by the architect Martín Nogueira. It showcases Sevillian Regionalist and eclectic elements, with characteristic ornamental façades, wrought iron balconies, and decorative ceramic details. The building is a notable example of early 20th-century urban architecture in the Casco Antiguo district, reflecting the stylistic trends and craftsmanship of the period.

data.name: Edificio de La Unión y el Fénix
data.style: Sevillian Regionalism with Neo-Baroque and Renaissance influences
data.description: The La Unión y el Fénix Building in Seville was constructed between 1926 and 1929 as the headquarters of the insurance company La Unión y el Fénix Español. Designed by architect José Espiau y Muñoz, it represents a mature phase of Sevillian Regionalist architecture applied to corporate use. The building is characterized by its monumental corner tower, rich ornamental decoration in brick and ceramics, wrought iron balconies, and its iconic sculptural group of the phoenix rising with Ganymede, symbolizing rebirth and strength. It forms part of the architectural ensemble that defines Plaza Nueva as a center of institutional and commercial power in early 20th-century Seville.

data.name: Oficina de Correos y Telégrafos de Sevilla
data.description: The Central Post Office and Telegraphs building of Seville was constructed between 1927 and 1930 as part of the city’s modernization process in the years leading up to the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition. Designed by Joaquín Otamendi y Machimbarrena, the building combines monumental composition with Regionalist and Neo-Mudéjar elements, employing brickwork, ceramic decoration, and historicist motifs. Conceived as a symbol of state presence and technological progress, it occupies a prominent position on Avenida de la Constitución, integrating modern communications infrastructure into Seville’s historic urban core.

data.name: Edificio Coliseo España
data.style: Monumental Eclecticism with Regionalist and Art Deco influences
data.address: Av. de la Constitución, 38, Casco Antiguo, 41001 Sevilla
data.description: The Coliseo España Building was constructed between 1929 and 1931 as a multifunctional venue combining cinema, theater, and commercial uses. Designed by architect Vicente Traver y Tomás, it reflects the transition in Spanish architecture from historicist regionalism to more modern stylistic expressions, incorporating elements of Eclecticism and Art Deco. Strategically located between Plaza Nueva and Calle Tetuán, the building played a significant role in Seville’s cultural life during the early 20th century, representing the emergence of modern leisure architecture in the city.

data.name: Edificio Santa Lucía
data.address: Av. de la Constitución, 25, Casco Antiguo, 41004 Sevilla
data.description: The Santa Lucía Building was constructed between 1918 and 1922 as the headquarters of the insurance company Santa Lucía. Designed by architect José Espiau y Muñoz, it is an early and refined example of Sevillian Regionalist architecture applied to corporate and commercial use. The building features a balanced composition with Neo-Renaissance influences, rich ornamental detailing in brick and ceramics, and a sober yet monumental façade that integrates harmoniously into the urban setting of Plaza Nueva. It represents the emergence of modern corporate architecture in Seville during the early 20th century.

data.name: Casa de viviendas para Antonio González
data.address: Av. de la Constitución, 26, Casco Antiguo, 41004 Sevilla
data.description: The residential building for Antonio González was designed in 1925 by José Espiau y Muñoz, one of the most prominent architects of early 20th-century Seville. The building exhibits Sevillian Regionalist architecture with eclectic influences, featuring ornate brickwork, ceramic details, and wrought-iron balconies. It represents the expansion of urban residential architecture in Seville during the 1920s, combining functionality with a refined aesthetic characteristic of Espiau y Muñoz's work.

data.name: Casa Álvaro Dávila
data.address: Avenida de la Constitución 14, 41001, Sevilla, Sevilla
data.description: Casa Álvaro Dávila is a historic residential building designed by José Espiau y Muñoz in 1910. It features Sevillian Regionalist architecture with eclectic influences, including decorative ceramic panels, wrought-iron balconies, and elegant brickwork. The building exemplifies early 20th-century urban residences in Seville, reflecting the architect’s distinctive style and attention to regional detail.

data.name: Parroquia de la Concepción Inmaculada
data.address: C. Cristo de la Sed, 41, 41005 Sevilla
data.description: The Parroquia de la Concepción Inmaculada was constructed in 1928 by architect Vicente Traver. Its architecture combines Sevillian Regionalist and Neo-Baroque elements, featuring brick façades, decorative ceramic panels, and elegant bell towers. It serves as an active parish church and is an important example of early 20th-century ecclesiastical architecture in Seville.

data.name: Estadio Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán
data.address: C. Sevilla Fútbol Club, s/n, 41005 Sevilla
data.description: Inaugurated in 1958, it is the home of Sevilla FC. Designed by Manuel Muñoz Monasterio, it hosted the 1982 World Cup semifinals and the 1986 European Cup Final. It is famous for its large mural on the main facade and its 'boiling' atmosphere, being a key symbol of the Nervión district.

data.name: Hospital San Juan de Dios
data.description: Founded in 1943 in a villa called 'Villa Amalia', the current complex was developed between 1946 and 1951 by architect Manuel Galnares Sagastizábal. Originally a sanatorium for children with polio, it is managed by the Hospitaller Order of Saint John of God. It recently underwent a major architectural renovation completed in 2022, blending its historical mission with avant-garde healthcare facilities.

data.name: Antiguo Matadero Municipal
data.address: Av. de Ramón y Cajal, s/n, 41005 Sevilla
data.description: A masterpiece of Sevillian industrial architecture, the complex was designed by José Sáez y López in the Neomudéjar style. Built with red brick and ceramic tiles, it originally served as the city slaughterhouse. Today, it has been repurposed as an educational complex, housing the Delegación de Educación and the 'Cristóbal de Morales' Conservatory of Music.

data.architect: Ahmad Ben Baso (Almohad) / Unknown (19th century pavilion)
data.name: Centro Cívico Buhaira (Palacio de la Buhaira)
data.address: Av. de la Buhaira, s/n, 41018 Sevilla
data.description: The Buhaira complex is a historic site that houses the remains of an ancient Almohad 'almunia' (country estate) from the 12th century, including its original large pool. The current palace is a Neo-Mudéjar pavilion built in the late 19th century. Today, it serves as a municipal civic center and is surrounded by gardens that replicate the original Andalusian orchard layout.

data.name: Cimientos de la Basílica de la Milagrosa (Proyecto Inacabado)
data.description: The unfinished foundations of what was intended to be a colossal Neo-Gothic basilica, a project by Aníbal González that aimed to be his masterpiece. Construction began in 1928 but was halted after the architect's death in 1929 and a subsequent lack of funding. Today, the massive foundations remain as a testament to the ambitious scale of the project, partially occupied by the current Parroquia de la Milagrosa.

data.architect: Juan de Oviedo y de la Bandera
data.name: Parroquia de San Benito Abad
data.description: The Church of San Benito Abad was originally part of a Benedictine monastery founded after the Reconquista. The current building, completed in 1612, is a masterpiece of Sevillian Mannerism designed by Juan de Oviedo. It is famously the headquarters of the Hermandad de San Benito, one of the most traditional brotherhoods of Seville's Holy Week.

data.name: Centro Cívico Las Sirenas (Casa de las Sirenas)
data.description: A French-style palatial mansion built in the mid-19th century. Its name comes from the two sphinxes (often called mermaids by locals) that guard its entrance. After decades of neglect and near-demolition, it was restored in the 1990s and converted into a civic center. It stands out for its romantic garden and its unique aesthetic, which contrasts with the surrounding Mudejar and Baroque architecture of Seville.

data.architect: Unknown (Promoted by Marta de Jesús Carrillo and Beatriz Jerónima de la Concepción)
data.name: Iglesia del Pozo Santo
data.description: Part of the Hospital del Pozo Santo, founded in 1667 by the Franciscan Tertiaries. The church was consecrated in 1682 and is dedicated to the Christ of Sorrows. It is a prime example of Sevillian Baroque, featuring a simple yet elegant facade. The hospital has historically served as a home for elderly and disabled women, a mission that continues to this day.

data.name: Palacio de Bucarelli (Palacio de los Condes de Santa Coloma)
data.description: Built at the end of the 17th century by the Bucarelli family, prominent Florentine merchants who settled in Seville. It is considered one of the most important Baroque palaces in the city, featuring a magnificent main courtyard with marble columns and an extensive private garden. It remains a private residence but hosts cultural events and tours, preserving its original architectural layout and noble atmosphere.

data.name: Cine Cervantes (Antiguo Teatro Cervantes)
data.description: Originally built as a theater in 1873, it is one of the oldest and most emblematic cinemas in Seville. Designed by Juan Talavera de la Vega, it features a classic Italian-style theater layout with stalls and balconies. It has survived the decline of historical cinemas in the city center and remains a key cultural landmark, known for its grand screen and historic atmosphere.

data.name: Convento de Santa Rosalía
data.description: A Capuchin convent founded in the early 18th century. The church is a masterpiece of Sevillian Baroque, designed by Diego Antonio Díaz. It is renowned for its impressive altarpieces by Cayetano de Acosta, particularly the main one, which is considered one of the finest examples of the 18th-century Baroque style in the city. The exterior features a sober yet elegant brick facade typical of the San Lorenzo neighborhood.

data.name: Baños de la Reina Mora
data.description: A remarkably preserved Almohad-era hammam (public bath) from the 12th century. Despite being later converted for various uses, including a convent and a laundry, it still maintains its original vaulted structure and skylights (lucernas). It is one of the most important Almohad civil remains in Seville and was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural. Today, it is managed by the Hermandad de la Vera Cruz and open for cultural visits.

data.name: Antigua Residencia de la familia Font de Anta
data.description: The historic home of the Font de Anta family, a lineage of fundamental musicians for Seville's Holy Week. Manuel Font de Anta, composer of the famous march 'Amarguras', lived here. The house is a classic example of Sevillian domestic architecture from the 19th century, featuring a traditional courtyard and a brick facade that maintains the authentic character of the San Vicente neighborhood.

data.name: Parroquia de San Vicente Mártir
data.description: One of the historic parishes established after the Christian conquest. While its structure is Gothic-Mudéjar from the 14th century, it underwent significant Baroque transformations in the 18th century, including the addition of the Sacramental Chapel by Diego Antonio Díaz. It houses exceptional artworks, such as paintings by Pedro de Villegas Marmolejo and Francisco de Herrera the Elder, and is the seat of several traditional Holy Week brotherhoods.

data.architect: Juan de Oviedo y de la Bandera
data.name: Museo de Bellas Artes de Sevilla (Antiguo Convento de la Merced)
data.description: Considered the second most important art gallery in Spain. The building was originally the Convent of the Merced Calzada, completed in 1612. Its architecture revolves around three magnificent courtyards and a grand staircase. The church of the convent, now part of the museum, features a spectacular barrel vault and houses masterpieces by Murillo, Zurbarán, and Valdés Leal, making it the epicenter of the Sevillian School of painting.

data.name: Iglesia de San Gregorio (Padres Mercedarios)
data.description: A historic Baroque church rebuilt in 1758. Originally part of an English Jesuit college (San Gregorio Magno), it was later occupied by the Mercedarian Order. The interior features a single nave with a beautiful barrel vault and a notable main altarpiece. Its location on Alfonso XII street makes it a quiet but significant stop for those exploring the transition between the modern commercial center and the historic San Lorenzo neighborhood.

data.name: Iglesia de San Antonio Abad
data.description: A unique Baroque complex consisting of two interconnected churches. The current structure, completed around 1730 by the architect Diego Antonio Díaz, serves as the headquarters of the Hermandad del Silencio, the oldest 'primitive' brotherhood of Seville's Holy Week. Its interior is richly decorated with Baroque altarpieces and maintains a solemn atmosphere that is central to the city's religious identity.

data.name: Palacio de Monsalves
data.description: A grand palatial house that underwent a profound transformation in 1907 by the renowned architect Aníbal González. It stands out for its magnificent central courtyard with high-quality tiling and its elegant facade. Historically, it was the headquarters of the Presidency of the Junta de Andalucía and is currently planned to become an expansion of the nearby Museum of Fine Arts.

data.architect: Juan de Oviedo y de la Bandera
data.name: Convento del Santo Ángel (Carmelitas Descalzos)
data.description: A prominent Carmelite convent completed in 1610 (church inaugurated in 1608), designed by the master Juan de Oviedo. It is a fundamental example of the transition from Mannerism to Baroque in Seville. The church is famous for its extraordinary collection of sculptures, including works by Martínez Montañés and Juan de Mesa. Its museum, the Museo del Santo Ángel (MUSAN), houses one of the best collections of religious art in Andalusia.

data.name: Capilla del Mayor Dolor
data.description: A charming chapel located in the historic Plaza de Molviedro. Originally part of an 18th-century hospital (Compás de la Laguna), it was almost lost and later rebuilt in 1924. It is the canonical seat of the Brotherhood of 'Jesús Despojado'. The chapel stands out for its intimate atmosphere and its neoclassical altar. Its location in the El Arenal neighborhood reflects the historical urban renewal of the former 'Laguna de la Feria' area.

data.architect: Bernardo de Bustamante (Original) / Rafael de la Hoz (Renovation)
data.name: Capilla de la Piedad (Hermandad del Baratillo)
data.description: A historic chapel located in the El Arenal neighborhood, closely linked to the bullfighting tradition due to its proximity to the Maestranza bullring. Originally built in 1693 on a burial ground for plague victims, it underwent a significant expansion in 1963 by architect Rafael de la Hoz to accommodate the increase in devotees. It is the seat of the 'El Baratillo' brotherhood and houses the revered images of the Virgen de la Piedad and the Cristo de la Misericordia.

data.architect: Unknown (Commissioned by Alfonso X the Wise)
data.name: Reales Atarazanas de Sevilla
data.description: The Royal Shipyards of Seville are a prime example of medieval industrial architecture. Built in 1252 by order of King Alfonso X, the complex consisted of 17 large brick vaulted naves designed for the construction of galleys. Over the centuries, it has served as a customs house, artillery warehouse, and social center. It is currently undergoing a major restoration to become a prominent cultural hub, preserving its monumental brick arches and its direct historical link to the city's maritime past.

data.name: Plaza del Cabildo
data.description: A unique semicircular square designed by Joaquín Barquín y Barrón in the late 1940s. It features a continuous building with an arcaded gallery supported by marble columns and decorated with frescoes by José Palomar. On the straight side of the square, a well-preserved section of the Almohad inner wall (1184) can be seen. It is famous for its numismatic and philatelic market held every Sunday and for its quiet, elegant atmosphere in the heart of the city.

data.architect: Sebastián Van der Borcht (Original) / Juan Talavera y Heredia (Reforms)
data.name: Antiguo Edificio de la Real Casa de la Moneda (Agencia Tributaria)
data.description: Part of the historic Royal Mint (Casa de la Moneda) complex. Originally designed by the military engineer Sebastián Van der Borcht in the 18th century, it was later integrated into the city's modern administrative structure. The building features a solid neoclassical design with stone and brick elements. Its location near the Archivo de Indias and the Cathedral marks the transition from the old maritime Seville to the colonial administrative center.

data.name: Torre de la Plata
data.description: An octagonal defensive tower built in 1221 by the Almohads. It was part of the city's defensive walls that connected the Alcázar with the Torre del Oro. Originally, it protected the 'Postigo del Carbón'. For centuries, it was hidden by annexed buildings until its partial restoration in the 20th century. It is a key testimony to the late Almohad military architecture in Seville and is currently located in a picturesque courtyard accessible from Calle Santander.

data.name: Parroquia de Santa Cruz
data.description: The current church was built between 1665 and 1728 as the church of the Convent of the Holy Spirit. After the French occupation and the demolition of the original Santa Cruz church, the parish moved here in the 19th century. Its facade is a notable example of the transition from Mannerism to Baroque. Inside, it houses high-quality altarpieces and is the headquarters of the 'Santa Cruz' brotherhood, one of the most representative of the neighborhood's Holy Week.

data.architect: Unknown (Original 16th Century) / Manuel de la Lastra (20th Century Restoration)
data.name: Casa de Salinas
data.description: A stunning 16th-century palace located in the heart of the Santa Cruz neighborhood. Built in 1577 by Baltasar de Jaén, it reflects the wealth of the Golden Age of Seville. The house features a magnificent central courtyard with Renaissance arches, intricate Mudéjar plasterwork, and Roman mosaics brought from Itálica. It underwent a meticulous restoration in the early 20th century by Manuel de la Lastra, preserving its domestic character as a private residence while opening its doors for cultural visits.

data.name: Iglesia de Santa María de la Piedad (Convento de las Mercedarias Descalzas)
data.description: A beautiful Baroque church belonging to the Convent of the Discalced Mercedarians. Built between 1617 and 1625 by Juan de Segarra, it is a classic example of a convent church with a single nave. The interior is a hidden treasure of Sevillian art, featuring a magnificent main altarpiece and walls covered in paintings and Baroque decorations that create a deeply spiritual atmosphere. It is located in the historic San Bartolomé neighborhood, one of the most quiet and authentic areas of the old city.

data.architect: Unknown (Attributed to the circle of Ventura Rodríguez)
data.name: Casa Palacio San José
data.description: An elegant 18th-century palatial house that stands as a magnificent example of Sevillian civil architecture. It features a grand white marble entrance that leads to a traditional central courtyard surrounded by columns and arches. The building has been meticulously restored to serve as luxury accommodation, preserving original elements like its high ceilings and intricate ironwork. Its location in the San Bartolomé neighborhood highlights the historical evolution of the city's private residences.

data.name: Casa Palacio La Casa Blanca
data.description: A magnificent 18th-century palatial house that has been carefully restored to showcase its original architectural splendor. The building features a classic white facade that gives it its name, a grand entrance with marble details, and a central courtyard that is the heart of the residence. Its restoration in 2020 preserved the high wood-beamed ceilings and traditional tiling, blending historical charm with modern luxury. It represents the revitalization of the San Bartolomé neighborhood as a center for high-end heritage tourism.

data.architect: Pedro de Díaz de Palacios / Juan de Simancas
data.name: Convento de Madre de Dios de la Piedad
data.description: A magnificent Dominican convent founded in the late 15th century. The current church, built between 1551 and 1572, is a masterpiece of the Sevillian Renaissance. It features a spectacular Mudéjar coffered ceiling and a grand portal designed by Juan de Oviedo the Elder. Historically, it was the burial place for descendants of Christopher Columbus and Hernán Cortés. Today, it remains an active cloistered convent famous for its traditional handmade sweets.

data.name: Torre de Don Fadrique
data.description: A remarkable free-standing defensive and residential tower built in 1252 by order of Infante Don Fadrique, son of King Ferdinand III. It is a rare example of Gothic architecture in Seville, featuring Romanesque elements and a square floor plan. Legend associates the tower with a tragic romance between the Infante and Queen Joanna. Standing within the gardens of the Monastery of Santa Clara, it has three levels and provides an essential link to the early years of the Christian reconquest of the city.

data.name: Edificio Singer (Nave Singer)
data.description: Built in 1913 by the renowned architect José Espiau y Muñoz, this building was originally a workshop and warehouse for the Singer sewing machine company. It is a prime example of early 20th-century industrial architecture in Seville, featuring a brick facade with ceramic decorations. The project was commissioned by the industrialist Nicanor Balbontín. After decades of neglect, it was restored in 1998 and currently serves as a training center and municipal school-workshop, preserving its distinctive industrial heritage near the Alameda de Hércules.

data.name: Capilla de la Santa Cruz del Rodeo y Nuestra Señora del Carmen
data.description: A modest and traditional chapel located near the ancient 'Rodeo' area of Seville. Its origins date back to the 17th century, though it underwent significant aesthetic changes during the 18th century. It is the seat of the Brotherhood of the 'Santa Cruz del Rodeo', which has deep roots in the local neighborhood. The simple facade features a small belfry and ceramic tiles depicting the Virgin, representing the popular and intimate religious architecture of Seville's historic suburbs.

data.name: Iglesia de San Nicolás de Bari
data.description: Situada en el corazón de la antigua judería, esta iglesia es uno de los mejores ejemplos del barroco sevillano del siglo XVIII. Aunque su origen es medieval (tras la conquista de 1248), el templo actual fue bendecido en 1758. Destaca por su planta de cinco naves separadas por columnas de mármol rojo y sus ricas yeserías policromadas. Es especialmente famosa por albergar a la Hermandad de la Candelaria y por su retablo mayor, una obra maestra de la transición al neoclasicismo.

data.name: Casas para Laureano Montoto
data.address: Calle Alfonso XII, 27-29 (esquina con Almirante Ulloa)
data.description: Este conjunto de viviendas fue proyectado por un joven Aníbal González para Laureano Montoto. Es uno de los ejemplos más puros de modernismo en Sevilla, rompiendo con la tradición de la época. Destaca por el uso del ladrillo visto, los juegos de curvas en la fachada, los miradores acristalados y la rica decoración cerámica. El edificio marca el inicio de la renovación arquitectónica de la ciudad a principios del siglo XX, mostrando influencias de la vanguardia europea adaptadas al contexto local.

data.name: Setas de Sevilla (Metropol Parasol)
data.address: Plaza de la Encarnación, s/n, 41003 Sevilla
data.description: Considered the largest wooden structure in the world, this avant-garde project revitalized the Plaza de la Encarnación. It consists of six large mushroom-shaped parasols whose design was inspired by the vaults of the Seville Cathedral and the ficus trees in the Plaza del Cristo de Burgos. The complex houses the Antiquarium Museum (Roman and Visigothic archaeological remains) in its basement, a fresh food market, an elevated square for events, and a panoramic viewpoint with a winding walkway offering spectacular views of the entire city.

data.name: Antigua Estación de Córdoba (Plaza de Armas)
data.address: Plaza de la Legión, s/n, 41001 Sevilla
data.description: Inspired by the Great Mosque of Córdoba and the Alhambra in Granada, this former railway station is a masterpiece of Neo-Mudejar architecture combined with 19th-century iron engineering. Built for the MZA railway company, its main facade features red and white brickwork and horseshoe arches, while the interior is covered by a magnificent iron and glass vault. After the 1992 Universal Exposition, it was repurposed into a shopping mall and cinema complex, carefully preserving its historic structure as a key landmark of Seville's industrial and architectural heritage near the Guadalquivir river.

data.name: Torre Sevilla
data.description: Standing at 180.5 meters tall, Torre Sevilla is the first skyscraper in the city and the tallest building in Andalusia. Designed by the prestigious Argentine architect César Pelli, its elliptical structure is clad in terracotta-colored aluminum, reflecting the traditional ceramics of the nearby Triana neighborhood. The tower serves as a multifunctional complex, housing offices, a luxury hotel, and a panoramic terrace at the top known as 'Atalaya'. It represents the modern expansion of Seville's skyline on the Isla de la Cartuja, standing as a controversial yet iconic symbol of 21st-century urban development.

data.name: Monasterio de Santa María de las Cuevas (La Cartuja)
data.description: This historic monastery has lived many lives: from a Carthusian spiritual retreat where Christopher Columbus stayed and was initially buried, to a world-renowned ceramics factory (Pickman) in the 19th century, and finally the Royal Pavilion during the Expo '92. Its architecture is a unique blend of Gothic, Mudejar, and Renaissance styles, featuring iconic brick chimneys from its industrial era. Today, it serves as the headquarters of the Andalusian Center for Contemporary Art (CAAC), merging centuries of history with avant-garde artistic expressions.

data.name: Pabellón del Siglo XV
data.address: Camino de los Descubrimientos, s/n, 41092 Sevilla
data.description: Built for the 1992 Universal Exposition, this pavilion was designed to bridge the gap between the historic Carthusian monastery and the modern Expo site. Its architecture is characterized by its sobriety and the use of light, featuring large open spaces and a minimalist aesthetic. During the Expo, it housed artifacts and exhibits related to the 15th century and the Age of Discovery. Today, it remains part of the Andalusian Center for Contemporary Art (CAAC) complex, often used for temporary exhibitions and cultural events, maintaining its role as a link between Seville's storied past and its modern identity.

data.name: Capilla de Santa Ana
data.description: Located within the Monastery of Santa María de las Cuevas, this chapel is historically significant as the initial burial place of Christopher Columbus before his remains were moved to Santo Domingo. Its architecture reflects the transition from Gothic to Mudejar, featuring a modest yet spiritually powerful space. The chapel was a private place of prayer for the Carthusian monks and remains one of the most evocative corners of the monastic complex, symbolizing the deep connections between the monastery and the era of great maritime discoveries.

data.name: Pabellón de Marruecos (Pabellón Hassan II)
data.description: Originally built as the Moroccan Pavilion for the Expo '92, this building is a masterpiece of traditional Moroccan craftsmanship. Designed by Michel Pinseau, it was a gift from King Hassan II to the city of Seville. The structure features a star-shaped floor plan and was handcrafted by hundreds of Moroccan artisans using traditional techniques such as 'zellige' tilework, carved plaster (stucco), and cedar wood ceilings. Today, it serves as the headquarters of the Three Cultures of the Mediterranean Foundation, standing as a permanent symbol of cultural exchange and one of the best-preserved pavilions from the World Fair.

data.name: Antiguo Pabellón de Kuwait
data.description: Designed by the renowned architect Santiago Calatrava, this pavilion was one of the most innovative structures of Expo '92. It is famous for its kinetic roof, consisting of 17 massive curved wooden ribs that could open and close like palm fronds or a ribcage, responding to the sun and light. The base is made of translucent glass and white concrete, creating a luminous interior space. Although the mechanism that moved the roof is no longer in regular use, the building remains a prime example of Calatrava’s sculptural and structural style, currently serving as a modern office and event space in the Cartuja Science and Technology Park.

data.name: Cohete Ariane 4
data.description: This full-scale replica of the Ariane 4 rocket was one of the major attractions of the 1992 Universal Exposition, donated by the European Space Agency (ESA). Standing at over 50 meters tall, it represents Europe's success in the space race and technological innovation during the late 20th century. Located near the former Pavilion of the Future, the rocket remains a powerful symbol of the Isla de la Cartuja's transformation into a hub for science and technology. It serves as a nostalgic landmark for locals and visitors alike, reminding the city of the global impact of the Expo '92.

data.name: Pabellón del Futuro
data.address: Camino de los Descubrimientos, s/n, 41092 Sevilla
data.description: Designed by the MBM studio in collaboration with the renowned structural engineer Peter Rice, the Pavilion of the Future was one of the thematic highlights of Expo '92. Its most striking feature is its enormous stone facade made of massive granite blocks and its high-tech roof structures. The building was designed to represent human progress and future challenges in science and technology. Today, it remains a vital part of Seville's scientific landscape, housing the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC) and the General Archive of Andalusia, standing as a testament to the enduring architectural legacy of the Universal Exposition.
