Its most striking feature is its enormous stone facade made of massive granite blocks and its high-tech roof structures. The building was designed to represent human progress and future challenges in science and technology. Today, it remains a vital part of Seville's scientific landscape, housing the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC) and the General Archive of Andalusia, standing as a testament to the enduring architectural legacy of the Universal Exposition.

data.name: Pabellón de Canadá
data.description: Designed by architect Bing Thom, the Canada Pavilion was one of the most popular attractions of Expo '92, famous for its massive IMAX theatre and its innovative cooling system. The building features a clean, white geometric design clad in zinc panels, a nod to Canada's role as a leading zinc exporter. Its interior courtyard and cascading water walls were designed to provide a cool refuge from the Seville heat, lowering the temperature by up to 10 degrees Celsius naturally. Today, the building has been successfully repurposed as the headquarters of the EOI Business School (Escuela de Organización Industrial), preserving its architectural legacy while serving as a center for higher education.

data.name: Pabellón de Italia
data.description: Designed by the prestigious architects Gae Aulenti and Pierluigi Spadolini, the Italy Pavilion was the largest national pavilion at Expo '92. It was conceived as a 'fortress of knowledge,' featuring a massive, fortress-like structure with high walls and a central courtyard. The building is known for its use of traditional materials like stone and terracotta combined with modern steel and glass elements. Its design pays homage to the Italian urban tradition of the 'piazza' and the 'palazzo'. After the Expo, it was repurposed to house several technology companies and institutions within the Cartuja Science and Technology Park, maintaining its imposing presence as a landmark of international cooperation and architectural excellence.

data.architect: Jean-Paul Viguier, Jean-François Jodry & François Seigneur
data.name: Pabellón de Francia
data.description: Designed by the architects Viguier, Jodry, and Seigneur, the France Pavilion was a standout feature of Expo '92, known for its massive 50x50 meter mirrored canopy that covered a large public square. Below this 'floating' roof, a deep well known as the 'Wells of Images' descended several floors, offering a unique multimedia experience. The building also pioneered a natural air-conditioning system using a thin film of water on the ground to cool the air. Today, it has been repurposed as a business incubator and technological hub ('El Cubo' by Telefónica), successfully integrating its avant-garde 1992 design into the modern Cartuja Science and Technology Park.

data.architect: Monark Group (Juha Jääskeläinen, Juha Kaakko, Petri Rouhiainen, Matti Sanaksenaho & Jari Tirkkonen)
data.name: Pabellón de Finlandia (La Garganta del Infierno)
data.description: Widely regarded as one of the architectural gems of Expo '92, the Finland Pavilion consists of two contrasting structures: 'The Machine' (made of steel) and 'The Keel' (crafted from warm, traditional Finnish pine wood). These two buildings are separated by a narrow, dramatic corridor only 15 meters wide, inspired by the Helvetinjärvi gorge in Finland. This design represented the dialogue between nature and technology. The pavilion won numerous awards for its minimalist and evocative approach. Today, it is beautifully preserved and serves as the headquarters of the Foundation for Technological Innovation (COTEC), maintaining its status as a masterpiece of contemporary design.

data.name: Antiguo Pabellón de Nueva Zelanda
data.description: The New Zealand Pavilion was one of the most evocative of Expo '92, featuring a dramatic facade that replicated a 14-meter-high New Zealand cliff, complete with native vegetation and a waterfall. This 'living' wall hid a modern interior housing exhibits and a performance space for the Haka, performed daily by a Maori group. Designed by Ian Athfield, the pavilion aimed to represent the rugged beauty of the New Zealand landscape and its maritime heritage. Although the cliff facade was removed after the exposition, the core building remains and has been converted into office spaces, currently serving as the headquarters for various technology companies.

data.name: Pabellón de España
data.address: Camino de los Descubrimientos, s/n (Isla de la Cartuja), 41092 Sevilla
data.description: Designed by architect Julio Cano Lasso, the Spain Pavilion was the central host building of Expo '92. It is characterized by its elegant and monumental design, featuring a large white cube balanced by a cylindrical tower and a beautiful colonnade. The building was strategically placed next to the Lake of Spain, serving as a symbolic heart for the national participation. Its interior housed grand exhibition halls, including the 'Treasures of Spanish Art' and a Moviemax theatre. After the Expo, the building has continued to serve as a prestigious venue for exhibitions and institutional events, and it is currently part of the Isla Mágica theme park area, maintaining its status as an architectural icon of the 1992 legacy.

data.name: Avenida de Europa (Expo '92)
data.address: Calle Isaac Newton (Isla de la Cartuja), 41092 Sevilla
data.description: The Avenida de Europa was the symbolic and functional backbone of the international area at Expo '92. This grand promenade was famous for its twelve massive 'bioclimatic towers' (designed by Hennin and Normier), which served as architectural landmarks and technical devices to cool the environment through micronized water spray. Each tower represented a member state of the then European Economic Community. The avenue connected the pavilions of various nations and featured lush landscaping, shaded areas, and a lively atmosphere. Today, while the towers and the original layout have been modified, it remains a central thoroughfare of the Cartuja Science and Technology Park, keeping the spirit of European integration alive.

data.name: Antiguo Pabellón de Turquía
data.address: Calle Isaac Newton, s/n (Isla de la Cartuja), 41092 Sevilla
data.description: Designed by architect Doruk Pamir, the Turkey Pavilion was a striking example of modern architecture at Expo '92. It stood out for its large red steel structure and its high-tech aesthetic, which contrasted with traditional Turkish elements presented inside. The building was designed to be easily assembled and disassembled, featuring a light and airy feel. After the Universal Exposition, it was integrated into the Cartuja Science and Technology Park. Today, it has been renovated and repurposed as office space for various technology and service companies, maintaining its distinctive red structural elements as a reminder of its original role.

data.name: Pabellón de Andalucía
data.description: Designed by architect Juan Ruesga Navarro, the Andalusia Pavilion was a flagship building of Expo '92, symbolizing the host region's identity. Its design is famous for the large cylinder clad in white Macael marble that appears to be tilted or emerging from a blue ceramic-tiled base, representing the integration of tradition and modernity. Located in a prime spot near the lake, it was one of the most visited pavilions, showcasing the culture, history, and future of Andalusia. After the World Fair, the building was chosen as the headquarters for the Radio and Television of Andalusia (RTVA) and Canal Sur, ensuring its preservation as one of the most iconic and well-maintained landmarks of the 1992 legacy.

data.name: Edificio Expo (Antiguo World Trade Center)
data.address: Calle Américo Vespucio, 1 (Isla de la Cartuja), 41092 Sevilla
data.description: Designed by architect Antonio Vázquez de Castro, this building was the World Trade Center during Expo '92, acting as the main hub for international trade and administrative coordination. Its architecture is characterized by its large glass surfaces and its distinctive pyramid-shaped skylights that flood the interior with natural light. The building was designed to be a highly functional and flexible office space, equipped with the latest technology of the time. Today, it remains one of the most important business centers in the Cartuja Science and Technology Park, hosting numerous technology companies and institutions, and stands as a key example of the successful repurposing of Expo '92's infrastructure.

data.name: Pabellón de México
data.description: Designed by the prestigious architect Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, the Mexico Pavilion for Expo '92 was a modern reinterpretation of traditional Mayan pyramids. The building is famous for its X-shaped steel structure on the roof and its distinctive facades decorated with reliefs and motifs that reflect Mexico's rich pre-Columbian history. During the fair, it showcased a blend of ancient treasures and modern technological achievements. Today, the pavilion is perfectly preserved and serves as a center for several institutions, including the Andalusian Society for the Development of the Information Society (SADIEL), standing as a vibrant example of the 1992 architectural legacy.

data.name: Pabellón de Chile
data.description: Designed by Germán del Sol and José Cruz, the Chile Pavilion was one of the most talked-about structures of Expo '92. It achieved international fame for housing a massive 60-ton iceberg brought directly from the Antarctic to the scorching heat of Seville, symbolizing Chile's environmental purity and technological capability. The building itself is a masterpiece of wooden architecture, constructed with laminated pine beams and featuring a design inspired by traditional Chilean barns and boats. The undulating wooden skin was designed to allow natural ventilation. Today, it remains as an office building, standing as one of the best examples of sustainable and expressive wood construction from the exposition.

data.name: Pabellón de Mónaco
data.description: Designed by architect Fabrice Notari, the Monaco Pavilion was a tribute to the Principality's deep connection with the sea. Its facade is a faithful recreation of the entrance to the famous Oceanographic Museum of Monaco, standing out with its neoclassical elegance amidst the modern structures of the Expo. During the fair, its main attraction was a large aquarium that showcased Mediterranean marine life. Unlike many other pavilions, it has been perfectly preserved and continues to fulfill a similar role today as the 'Estación de Ecología Acuática Alberto I de Mónaco' (managed by Emasesa). It houses a 400,000-liter aquarium dedicated to the study of the flora and fauna of the Guadalquivir river, serving as a center for research and environmental education.

data.name: Pabellón de la Naturaleza
data.address: Camino de los Descubrimientos, s/n, 41092 Sevilla
data.description: The Nature Pavilion was one of the thematic pillars of Expo '92, designed to highlight the importance of biodiversity and environmental conservation. Its most famous feature was the 'Amazonian Bubble' (Burbuja Amazónica), a large greenhouse that recreated a tropical rainforest environment. The building is strategically located next to the Guadalquivir river and the American Garden (Jardín Americano). Today, the pavilion is divided into two functional areas: one part serves as the Consulate General of the Kingdom of Morocco in Seville, while the other houses the Environmental Education Center (Centro de Educación Ambiental), continuing its original mission of promoting ecological awareness.

data.architect: Manuel Graça Dias & Egas José Vieira
data.name: Pabellón de Portugal
data.description: Designed by architects Manuel Graça Dias and Egas José Vieira, the Portugal Pavilion was a bold statement of modern lusophone identity during Expo '92. Located in a prime spot near the Spain Pavilion, its design features clean, elegant lines and a distinctive blue and white facade. Under the theme 'Adventure of Centuries to Invent the Future,' it showcased Portugal's maritime history and its modern aspirations. In 1996, the Portuguese government donated the building to the city for a symbolic price. Since then, it has been perfectly preserved and currently serves as the headquarters for the Andalusian Energy Agency (Agencia Andaluza de la Energía), remaining one of the most active and well-kept buildings in the technology park.

data.name: Pabellón de Corea (Corea del Sur)
data.description: The South Korea Pavilion for Expo '92 was designed to resemble a 'Janchijip,' a traditional Korean house used for banquets and celebrations. Architect Hak-Sun Oh masterfully blended ancient symbols, like the 'Gate of Eternal Youth' at its entrance, with modern materials. A notable change after the Expo was the color of its exterior structural columns: they were originally a vibrant red and were later painted blue. Inside, it famously featured art by the pioneer of video art, Nam June Paik. Today, the building is in excellent condition and serves as the headquarters for Alter Technology, a leading firm in the aerospace and satellite industry, proving that even 'temporary' Expo architecture can have a long-lasting technological life.

data.architect: Segundo Cardona Colom, Luis Sierra y Alberto Ferrer (Sierra, Cardona & Ferrer)
data.name: Antiguo Pabellón de Puerto Rico
data.description: Designed by the firm Sierra, Cardona & Ferrer, the Puerto Rico Pavilion stands out for its bold geometric composition of three distinct volumes: a triangular stone block (evoking Puerto Rican military fortifications), a glass and copper cylinder with a metallic frame, and a modernist white glass pergola. During Expo '92, it was famous for its 360-degree IMAX cinema and art exhibitions featuring Caribbean masters. Interestingly, it originally featured a large mural named 'La isla recreada' by Susana Espinosa. After serving for years as a postal R&D center for Correos (whose faded logo can still be traced on the walls), it is now perfectly preserved and serves as the headquarters for the 'Instituto Andaluz de Administración Pública' (IAAP) of the Junta de Andalucía.

data.architect: José Ramón Moreno & Orestes del Castillo
data.name: Pabellón de Cuba
data.description: Designed by architects José Ramón Moreno and Orestes del Castillo, the Cuba Pavilion was a rectangular three-story structure that combined modern steel and glass with traditional Cuban materials. One of its most poetic features was the 'Tropical Garden' at the entrance, where 14 palm trees were planted to represent each of the Cuban provinces. During the fair, it showcased the country's history and its advances in biotechnology and medicine, presided over by a replica of 'La Giraldilla' (the symbol of Havana). After the Expo, the building was rehabilitated in 1998. Today, it remains in excellent condition and serves as the headquarters for VEIASA (Verificaciones Industriales de Andalucía), a public company of the Junta de Andalucía.

data.architect: Álvaro Navarro & Miguel M. de Castilla
data.name: Plaza de África (Pabellón de África Subsahariana)
data.description: The Plaza de África was a unique collective space at Expo '92, designed to host fifteen Sub-Saharan nations (including Angola, Cape Verde, Ivory Coast, Ethiopia, Gabon, Ghana, Guinea-Bissau, Kenya, Liberia, Nigeria, Senegal, Tanzania, Zaire, Zambia, and Zimbabwe). The complex consists of two main bodies connected by a closed walkway over a pond. Its architecture is characterized by geometric glass volumes and modular spaces that allowed each country to showcase its specific heritage within a unified African context. Today, the building has been successfully repurposed and serves as the prestigious headquarters of the CEA (Confederación de Empresarios de Andalucía), remaining one of the most active and best-preserved administrative buildings in the Cartuja Science and Technology Park.

data.architect: Jesús Castañón Díaz, Ernesto Sánchez Zapata y Juan Luis Gómez Estern
data.name: Plaza de América (Expo '92)
data.address: Camino de los Descubrimientos, s/n, 41092 Sevilla
data.description: The Plaza de América was the largest architectural complex built by the Spanish government for Expo '92, covering over 40,000 square meters. It was designed to house 16 American countries that did not have their own individual pavilions (such as Argentina, Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Guatemala, and others). The complex is organized into several large blocks named after Columbus's ships: La Pinta, La Niña, and La Santa María. After the exposition, it underwent a major renovation to become a permanent educational facility. Since 1997, it has been the home of the Escuela Superior de Ingeniería (Higher Technical School of Engineering) of the University of Seville, serving as a cornerstone of the academic life in the Cartuja Science and Technology Park.

data.name: Pabellón de Andalucía
data.description: El Pabellón de Andalucía fue el edificio insignia de la comunidad anfitriona durante la Expo '92. Su diseño es famoso por el gran cilindro inclinado revestido de mármol blanco de Macael, que parece emerger de una base de cerámica azul, simbolizando la unión entre la tradición artesana y la modernidad tecnológica. Situado en una posición privilegiada junto al Lago de España, fue uno de los pabellones más visitados, ofreciendo un viaje por la historia y el futuro de la región. Tras la muestra, el edificio se convirtió en la sede central de la Radio y Televisión de Andalucía (RTVA) y Canal Sur, lo que ha permitido que se mantenga en un estado de conservación impecable hasta hoy.

data.name: Pabellón de Cruzcampo
data.address: Calle José de Gálvez, s/n (Junto al Teatro Central), 41092 Sevilla
data.description: Designed by architect Miguel de Oriol e Ybarra, the Cruzcampo Pavilion was a vibrant social hub at Expo '92. Its architecture was characterized by a large copper-clad structure and a distinctive tower that reached 40 meters in height, serving as a lighthouse for visitors. The pavilion's terrace was one of the most coveted spots to watch the nightly lake show. A large statue of Gambrinus, the brand's iconic mascot, welcomed guests. Today, the building has a mixed use: it houses an Asian restaurant and a famous flamenco venue called 'El Palacio Andaluz'. Recently, the iconic Gambrinus statue has been the subject of restoration efforts to preserve it as a piece of the city's sentimental history.

data.architect: Pedro Ramírez Vázquez & Rafael de la Hoz
data.name: Pabellón del Comité Olímpico Internacional (COI)
data.address: Calle Matemáticos Rey Pastor y Castro, s/n, 41092 Sevilla
data.description: Designed by the prestigious architects Pedro Ramírez Vázquez (who also designed the Mexico Pavilion) and Rafael de la Hoz, the COI Pavilion was inspired by the simplicity of a Greek temple. Its roof featured the iconic Olympic rings, visible from the air. During Expo '92, it housed priceless works of art like Dalí's 'Cosmic Athlete' and a mural by Antoni Tàpies. A major highlight was the Olympic cauldron at its entrance, where the flame burned for all six months of the Expo—longer than during the actual Olympic Games. Today, the building has been significantly altered and serves as a nightlife venue (a well-known disco in the area), while its original cauldron was moved to the 'Glorieta Olímpica' near the Alamillo Bridge.

data.name: Pabellón de la Navegación
data.description: Designed by the renowned Seville architect Guillermo Vázquez Consuegra, this pavilion was the most visited thematic space of Expo '92, welcoming over 2 million people. Its architecture is deeply symbolic: the large curved wooden roof evokes the hull of an overturned ship, and the building itself is situated right on the edge of the Guadalquivir river, integrated with the pier. The interior was originally a vast, open space dedicated to the history of maritime exploration. Today, it has been brilliantly repurposed as a modern interactive museum that explores Seville's relationship with the sea and the Atlantic navigation. The complex also includes the 60-meter high Schindler Tower, which serves as a spectacular viewpoint over the city and the river.

data.name: Schindler Tower
data.address: Camino de los Descubrimientos, 2 (Next to the Pavilion of Navigation), 41092 Seville
data.description: Part of the Pavilion of Navigation complex, the Schindler Tower was designed as a tribute to modern engineering. Standing 65 meters tall, it is named after the Swiss elevator company Schindler, which installed its fastest panoramic lifts for the Expo (capable of reaching the top in just 24 seconds). The structure consists of two sleek stainless steel bodies rising over the Guadalquivir river. It currently remains open to the public as a viewpoint, offering one of the most breathtaking and comprehensive views of the Seville skyline, the river, and the entire Cartuja Science and Technology Park.

data.construction: 1904 (original brewery), current facilities expanded mid-20th century
data.name: Cruzcampo Brewery – Los Arcos
data.description: The Cruzcampo Brewery in Los Arcos is one of Seville’s most iconic industrial complexes and a key landmark in the city’s brewing history. Established in the early 20th century, the facility played a crucial role in the growth of the Cruzcampo brand and in the modernization of beer production in Andalusia. The site is characterized by functional industrial architecture, composed of large production halls, silos, and auxiliary buildings that reflect successive phases of expansion and technological adaptation. Beyond its manufacturing role, the brewery has gradually incorporated visitor and educational spaces, reinforcing its cultural and heritage value within the Los Arcos district and in Seville’s broader industrial legacy.

data.name: ONCE Pavilion
data.description: Designed by architects Gilbert Barbany and Sebastián Mateu, the ONCE Pavilion was conceived as a model of a 'barrier-free world.' The building consists of two large glass parallelepipeds connected by a central core. During Expo '92, it was famous for its 'path of sensations' where visitors could experience the daily challenges faced by people with disabilities through immersive, lightless rooms and 3D floating cinemas. The building's structure is supported by striking triangular metal frames that were originally blue and are now painted red. It was built as a permanent structure and continues to serve as the regional headquarters for the ONCE Foundation, remaining one of the most active and socially significant buildings in the Cartuja park.

data.type: Transport Infrastructure / Archeology of the Expo
data.name: Monorail Stations (Remains)
data.address: Calle Tomás Alva Edison (Main remains), 41092 Seville
data.description: The Expo '92 monorail was a 3.1 km elevated loop that offered panoramic views of the site. It featured three main stations: North (near Plaza de África), Central (near Kuwait Pavilion), and South (near Andalusia Pavilion). While the trains were sold and the tracks dismantled in 1993, some structures remain. The most visible vestige is the 'Estación Central' skeleton located on Calle Tomás Alva Edison; its concrete pillars and some mechanical ramps are still standing, overgrown with vegetation, serving as a 'modern ruin.' Interestingly, the original trains are still operational today, as they were bought and relocated to the 'Europa-Park' theme park in Germany (where they are known as the EP-Express).

data.name: Rank Xerox Pavilion
data.description: Designed by Manuel Carrilero, the Rank Xerox Pavilion was intended to be a permanent structure from its conception. Its most striking feature is a massive upper central frame that creates a hollow rectangular space, inspired by the shape of a prehistoric dolmen to symbolize humanity's earliest communicative structures. During Expo '92, it showcased the 'Company of the Document's' vision for the future, featuring cutting-edge laser printing and electronic publishing technologies. It was a must-visit for tech enthusiasts, who could even take home a color photocopy of their ID as a futuristic souvenir. Today, the building is perfectly preserved and serves as the headquarters for INERCO, a leading environmental engineering and consultancy firm.

data.architect: Luis Marín de Terán & Aurelio del Pozo
data.name: Press Building (Edificio de la Prensa)
data.description: Designed by the architects Luis Marín de Terán and Aurelio del Pozo, the Press Building was the nerve center for thousands of journalists from all over the world during Expo '92. Its design prioritized functionality and advanced telecommunications for the era. The building is characterized by its organized, office-like structure and its strategic location near the World Trade Center and the main entrances. It was one of the first buildings to be planned for permanent use after the event. Today, it remains perfectly operational and serves as an administrative office building, hosting various public institutions and departments of the Junta de Andalucía.

data.name: Torre Triana
data.address: Calle Juan Antonio de Vizarrón, s/n, 41092 Sevilla
data.description: Diseñada por el célebre arquitecto navarro Francisco Javier Sáenz de Oiza, Torre Triana es el edificio administrativo más grande de la Junta de Andalucía. Su diseño circular está inspirado en el Castillo de Sant'Angelo de Roma, con un enorme patio interior y una fachada de mármol amarillo de Almería que le da un tono dorado muy característico. Aunque se planificó durante la Expo '92, se terminó justo después para consolidar el uso administrativo de la isla. Con sus ocho plantas y su forma de anillo, es capaz de albergar a miles de funcionarios. Se encuentra estratégicamente situada a la entrada sur de la Cartuja, cerca del Pabellón de la Navegación.

data.architect: Antonio Cruz & Antonio Ortiz (Cruz y Ortiz Arquitectos)
data.name: Estadio La Cartuja
data.address: Isla de la Cartuja, Sector Norte, 41092 Sevilla
data.description: Designed by the prestigious Seville duo Cruz y Ortiz (the same architects behind the Rijksmuseum renovation and the Wanda Metropolitano), the Estadio La Cartuja was built for the 1999 World Athletics Championships. It is a 'Category 4' UEFA stadium with a capacity for 60,000 spectators. Known for its elegant and functionalist design, the stadium features a distinctive white fabric roof and a multi-level concrete structure. Although it was originally built to attract a major football team or host the Olympics, it has become the fixed venue for the Copa del Rey finals and a premier location for international concerts by icons like AC/DC, Bruce Springsteen, and Red Hot Chili Peppers. It is currently undergoing renovations to remove its athletics track and further increase its capacity for future international football tournaments.

data.name: Iglesia del Real Hospital de San Lázaro
data.description: The Church of the Royal Hospital of Saint Lazarus is part of one of the oldest hospital institutions in Seville, founded in the 13th century to treat leprosy. The current church, built in the 16th century, is a jewel of the Seville Mudejar style, featuring a beautiful altarpiece and a Renaissance portal attributed to Hernán Ruiz II. The hospital complex has been a silent witness to the city's sanitary evolution over centuries. Located near the Alamillo Bridge, it serves as a historic gateway between the traditional Macarena district and the modern Isla de la Cartuja. Today, it is recognized as a site of Cultural Interest (BIC), preserving its spiritual and architectural essence amidst the modern city.

data.name: Teatro Central (antiguamente Teatro Central Hispano)
data.description: Originally named 'Teatro Central Hispano' due to the sponsorship of Banco Central and Banco Hispano Americano, it was inaugurated in 1992 as the home for 'new scenic trends' during the Universal Exposition. Its design is famous for the concept of 'a box within a box': a black interior box (the stage and seating) tilted 5 degrees and inscribed within a larger, clean stone-clad cube. This minimalist and windowless exterior hides one of the most versatile stages in Europe, capable of changing its configuration (Italian, Elizabethan, or Arena style) to accommodate everything from experimental theatre and contemporary dance to jazz and flamenco. It is situated right on the banks of the Guadalquivir river, surrounded by lush vegetation that contrasts with its sharp, sober lines. Today, it remains a premier cultural reference in Andalusia for avant-garde performing arts.

data.name: Rank Xerox Pavilion (Edificio INERCO)
data.description: Diseñado por Manuel Carrilero de la Torre, el pabellón de Rank Xerox fue planeado para perdurar tras la Expo '92. Su arquitectura es profundamente simbólica: la estructura superior en forma de marco hueco está inspirada en un dolmen prehistórico, representando la primera gran actuación tecnológica y comunicativa del ser humano. Durante la muestra, el edificio albergó la 'Oficina del Futuro', donde los visitantes quedaban asombrados por las entonces novedosas impresoras láser y la edición electrónica. Un recuerdo icónico para muchos fue llevarse una fotocopia del DNI a color, una tecnología casi mágica en 1992. En la actualidad, el edificio se encuentra en perfecto estado y es la sede de la ingeniería ambiental INERCO.

data.name: Pabellón de Red Eléctrica de España
data.description: Designed by Mariano Bayón, this pavilion was conceived as a timeless and abstract structure, closer to an infrastructure project than a traditional building. It is famous for its 'wall-like' appearance, with a floating enclosure that uses translucent marble and glass to balance light, temperature, and acoustics. During Expo '92, its interior explained the complex process of electricity distribution and control. Because it was built to high permanent standards, it didn't need major renovations after the fair. Today, it remains the regional headquarters and control center for Red Eléctrica (REE) in Andalusia, standing as a perfectly preserved example of the minimalist architecture from the 90s.

data.name: Pabellón de Retevisión
data.description: The Retevisión Pavilion was a cornerstone of the technical infrastructure for Expo '92, designed to showcase Spain's modernization in broadcasting. Its most iconic feature is the 60-meter high lattice telecommunications tower, which became a landmark in the northern sector of the Cartuja. The building itself is a clean, white, cubic structure that originally housed the equipment needed to broadcast the Expo signals to the entire world. Inside, visitors could see the first high-definition television (HDTV) demonstrations in Spain. Today, the building is perfectly preserved and serves as the headquarters for Cellnex Telecom, continuing its original legacy as a key hub for telecommunications in the region.

data.name: Hotel Príncipe de Asturias (Barceló Sevilla Renacimiento)
data.address: Avenida Álvaro Alonso Barba, s/n, 41092 Sevilla
data.description: Designed by the renowned architect Javier Carvajal, this hotel was the official residence for heads of state and royalty during Expo '92. Its most distinctive feature is its circular architecture, consisting of three large white cylindrical blocks that symbolize the three caravels of Columbus: La Pinta, La Niña, and La Santa María. The buildings are organized around a bright, open atrium that was revolutionary for Seville at the time. Despite facing financial struggles shortly after the Expo, it was acquired by the Barceló Group and rebranded as the Barceló Sevilla Renacimiento. Today, it remains a 5-star flagship of the city's hospitality, seamlessly blending its Expo heritage with a modern role as a top-tier business and family destination near the Isla Mágica theme park.

data.name: La Andalucía de los Niños
data.address: Camino de los Descubrimientos (Next to Puente de la Barqueta), 41092 Sevilla
data.description: Originally designed for Expo '92, this 10,000-square-meter park featured a perfect 1:33 scale replica of Andalusia’s most iconic monuments, including the Giralda, the Alhambra, and the Mosque of Cordoba. It was a masterpiece of detail, complete with miniature railways and water bodies. After the Expo, it remained open as part of 'Isla Mágica' and later as an independent attraction. Unfortunately, in recent years it has fallen into a state of severe neglect. In late 2023, the Andalusian government began a process to reclaim the site due to the 'grave abandonment' of the miniatures. Despite its current ruined state, it remains a symbol of the didactic and playful spirit of the Exposition.

data.architect: Julio Cano Lasso (Surroundings) / Expo '92 Landscape Team
data.name: Lago de España
data.address: Isla de la Cartuja (Now within Isla Mágica), 41092 Seville
data.description: The Lago de España was the centerpiece of Expo '92, a massive artificial water body (covering approx. 40,000 m2) surrounded by the pavilions of Spain's Autonomous Communities and the grand Spanish National Pavilion. Every night, it hosted the 'Spectacle of the Lake', a ground-breaking multimedia show featuring laser beams, fireworks, water screens with film projections, and mobile platforms. After the Expo, the lake's surface was reduced by about a third to make room for the 'Isla Mágica' theme park. Today, it remains the park's central feature, used for daily shows and boat rides. The iconic 'Pasarela del Lago' (a suspension bridge) still crosses it, and as of 2026, it is undergoing a full restoration to preserve this piece of 20th-century engineering.

data.architect: Confederación Hidrográfica del Guadalquivir / Expo '92 Engineers
data.name: Esclusa del Canal de la Expo (Canal de los Descubrimientos)
data.address: Camino de los Descubrimientos (Next to Pabellón del Futuro), 41092 Seville
data.description: The lock (esclusa) was the gateway for maritime traffic into the Canal de los Descubrimientos during Expo '92. It allowed vessels, including historical replicas and modern tour boats, to transition between the living Guadalquivir river and the internal canal system that bordered the eastern side of the Expo site. This infrastructure was essential to maintain a stable water level within the canal, regardless of the river's tides. After the Expo, the canal was gradually decommissioned, and the lock gate system became inactive. While the area near the 'Pabellón del Futuro' has been partially rehabilitated for the General Archive of Andalusia, the lock remains as a silent industrial vestige, a reminder of the complex water engineering that made the 'Island' of Cartuja a true maritime experience.

data.name: Jardines del Guadalquivir
data.address: Camino de los Descubrimientos (Next to Auditorio Rocío Jurado), 41092 Seville
data.description: Spanning over 8 hectares along the riverbank, these gardens were designed by Jorge Subirana and Silvia Decorde as a 'living museum' for Expo '92. They are divided into thematic sections, including a water garden, a rose garden with 105 different species, and a maze. The park is also notable for its integration of contemporary art, featuring sculptures like 'No ma dejado' (a loop-shaped walkway) by Eva Lootz and a brick structure by Per Kirkeby. Despite their high botanical and artistic value, the gardens suffered decades of neglect and vandalism. However, as of late 2025 and 2026, there are active municipal plans to restore them as a major 'green lung' for the city, aiming to recover the fountains, lighting, and unique monuments that once made this place a serene paradise within the bustling Expo site.

data.architect: Huss Park Attractions (Engineering) / Realizada por Bremen
data.name: Torre Banesto (Torre ABC / Pirulí)
data.description: The Banesto Tower was the iconic lookout point of Expo '92. Standing at 92 meters (symbolizing the year of the Expo), it features a circular cabin that slowly ascended while rotating, offering 360-degree views of the site and the city of Seville. It was one of the first structures completed on the island and became a massive advertising pillar for the Banesto bank. After the fair, it operated as an attraction for 'Isla Mágica' and later received sponsorship from the ABC newspaper, which rebranded it as 'Torre ABC'. Although it is currently out of service and its cabin remains grounded, it stands as a nostalgic vertical landmark within the Guadalquivir Gardens, visible from almost anywhere in the city center.

data.name: Helipuerto de la Cartuja (LEEX)
data.description: Built in 1988 to provide high-speed access for dignitaries and VIPs during Expo '92, the Cartuja Heliport remains one of the few urban heliports in Spain. It consists of a circular landing pad (FATO), hangars, and a terminal building. During the 1992 fair, it was a symbol of exclusivity, connecting the 'Island' with other cities and airports. After the Expo, it maintained a low profile, primarily used by emergency services (061) and private flights. However, since late 2025, it has entered a new era under the management of World Aviation Group. It now serves as a modern hub for tourist flights over Seville, a flight academy for helicopter pilots, and corporate air transport, consolidating its role as a key logistics node in the south of the Cartuja park.
